bible.visualPremise: Flat 2D stickman explainer visuals that shift between imagined battlefield scenes, close museum object shots, and backstage/theatrical illustrations to show how an image was invented and spread.
bible.visualTone: clear, slightly wry and investigative — warm enough to feel familiar when showing the myth, precise and neutral when showing archaeological evidence.

styleContract.illustrationStyle: Simplified stickman/doodle explainer construction — circle heads, dot eyes, stick limbs, mitten hands — never a detailed or semi-realistic character
styleContract.lineLanguage: Uniform thin, clean black outlines of identical weight everywhere; no sketchiness, no variable line weight, no cross-hatching
styleContract.shapeLanguage: Simple geometric primitives — circles, rounded rectangles, straight or gently curved lines — never intricate or organic detail
styleContract.detailLevel: Minimal — enough to read instantly at a glance, never busy or cluttered
styleContract.shadingPolicy: None — flat solid fills only, no gradients, no soft shadow rendering, no highlights
styleContract.dimensionality: 2D flat, no 3D rendering, no depth shading, no perspective distortion beyond simple flat-layer staging
styleContract.realismLevel: Non-realistic, iconographic — identity is carried by a handful of discrete flat features, never facial realism
styleContract.backgroundStrategy: 2-3 flat color layers (background/midground/foreground), never a fully rendered or photographic environment
forbiddenStyleTraits: realistic anatomy, fingers, or necks on stickman characters
styleContract.colorStrategy: Assign a single dominant background band color per setting family and reserve bronze/iron accents specifically for artifact closeups. Viewer avatars and role archetypes reuse their canonical clothing colors consistently across scenes so viewers recognize roles at a glance.
styleContract.lightingStrategy: Flat, stage-like lighting: warm rim light for battlefield dusk, even neutral light for museum interiors, a single pale spotlight on stage, and cool daylight for bog/bronze-age sites. No gradients or shading, only flat color blocks to imply time/mood.

palette.environmentPaletteRules: Use one dominant background band color per scene family (battlefield = warm orange; museum = off-white; theater = deep maroon; bronze-age = muted teal). Foreground artifacts use bronze accent or muddy brown as appropriate. Characters use the muted clothing palette so artifacts stand out.
palette.contrastRules: Keep characters and objects in mid-to-high contrast against the background band; museum cases and artifact pedestals are pale grey against off-white walls for legibility.

hero.reasoning: The episode does not follow a single individual's throughline. It moves between a viewer-planted imagined moment, object-focused archaeology, and historical/artist vignettes. Visual continuity is carried by consistent role archetypes (the viewer avatars, a warrior type, an archaeologist, named historical figures) rather than a single hero.

world.architecture: simple flat silhouettes: low timber longhouses for exterior Viking references, plain modern museum gallery interiors with pedestals, and a proscenium theater arch for stage scenes.
world.geography: Northern European coastal hills and bog landscapes, neutral studio interiors for theater and studio shots.
world.era: mix of Viking Age (c. 8th–11th century), Bronze Age (c. 2nd–1st millennium BCE), and 19th-century/modern settings.
world.recurringEnvironmentConstruction: 2-3 flat layers: sky/background color band, a midground band with simple silhouette shapes (hillline, museum wall, stage arch), and a foreground area with small tangible props (a pedestal, a dug-up patch, a prop helmet).
world.environmentalColorRules: Backgrounds are muted single-color bands; foreground props use the episode's palette colors with no gradients or texture.
world.weatherTimeConventions: Battlefield scenes use warm late-afternoon orange band in the sky; museum interiors are cool neutral off-white walls; theater stage uses deep maroon background with stage spot pale rectangle.
historicalScientificConstraints: Do not depict rivets or attachment points on confirmed Viking-age helmets where none were reported (Gjermundbu helmet is a plain iron dome without horn sockets).
Bronze Age Veksø helmets are decorative thin bronze with prominent attached horns and must look delicate, not combat-ready.

objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: The Gjermundbu helmet: a rounded iron dome helmet with a spectacle-shaped eye guard and plain iron surface, clearly built for deflecting blows and without any horn attachments.
objectLanguage.promptBlock: The Gjermundbu helmet: a rounded iron dome helmet with a spectacle-shaped eye guard and plain iron surface, with no horn sockets or decorative horns.
objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Used repeatedly as the clearest, best-preserved Viking-age helmet example that contradicts the horned-helmet myth.

objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: The Veksø helmets: two thin bronze ceremonial helmets each fitted with long curved horns tipped by small round discs, dated to the Nordic Bronze Age and likely ritual rather than combat gear.
objectLanguage.promptBlock: The Veksø helmets: two thin bronze ceremonial helmets with long curved horns tipped with small round discs, delicate and decorative rather than combat-ready.
objectLanguage.whyRecurring: These Bronze Age horned helmets are the older ritual objects that later viewers and artists misapplied to Viking imagery.

objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: Wagner's horned stage helmet: a theatrical costume helmet with exaggerated curved horns designed for spectacle rather than historical accuracy.
objectLanguage.promptBlock: A Wagner-style horned stage helmet: a theatrical costume helmet with large exaggerated curved horns, clearly designed for spectacle.
objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Represents the 19th-century theatrical costume look that popularized horned Vikings to mass audiences.

graphicLanguage.backgroundBehavior: Clean, uncluttered flat backgrounds (often light/white or the episode's own environment palette) — never assumed to be white-only; the Production Bible's graphic language decides per episode
graphicLanguage.lineStyle: The exact same line weight and fill language as narrative scenes — a graphic must never look like a different visual universe from the story frames around it
graphicLanguage.arrowsConnectors: Simple flat-filled arrow shapes and thin connector lines, same line language as everything else
graphicLanguage.characterUseInsideGraphics: Stickman characters, objects, and simplified environments are explicitly ALLOWED and encouraged inside a graphic when they clarify the point — a graphic is a composition family, never a text-only template
graphicLanguage.whitespaceBehavior: Generous but not empty — whitespace isolates the one idea a graphic communicates, it is never filler
graphicLanguage.colorUse: Uses this episode's own palette (muted forest-green, warm orange, muddy brown, pale grey) as flat fills, consistent with narrative scenes — never a separate infographic color scheme.
graphicLanguage.diagramConventions: When comparing helmets, present two flat side-by-side object blocks with labels: left block for archaeological helmets (Gjermundbu) and right block for ritual/ceremonial helmets (Veksø), with a thin black divider line and small pale grey caption rectangles.
graphicLanguage.comparisonLayouts: Use horizontal two-panel comparisons for 'what they expected vs what we found' moments; each panel keeps the same background band color to focus attention on the object differences.
graphicLanguage.timelineConventions: A simple flat horizontal timeline with three labeled dots: 'Bronze Age (c. 1000 BCE)', 'Viking Age (c. 793–1066)', '19th-century Romanticism (c. 1800s)'. Use pale grey line and small muted ochre dots.
graphicLanguage.mapConventions: A minimalist coastline silhouette for Scandinavia with small pale location dots for finds (Gjermundbu in Norway, Veksø in Denmark) and pale grey labels.
graphicLanguage.symbolicMetaphorLanguage: Use a theatrical mask or marquee icon to symbolize 'stage/theatre invention' and a small magnifying glass icon to symbolize 'archaeological evidence'.
graphicLanguage.overlayTextBehavior: A short (<=5 word) exact phrase may be requested directly of the image model only when it is naturally part of the drawn artwork itself (e.g. a sign, a clock face) AND the configured renderer has demonstrated adequate text fidelity for this recipe — otherwise all text is composited as a deterministic overlay after the base image.

cameraLanguage.simplicityReadabilityRules: Every frame must read clearly at thumbnail size — avoid busy multi-subject compositions unless the beat's own visual concept specifically requires comparing multiple subjects at once
cameraLanguage.framingConventions: Establishing shots: wide two-thirds background band with small stickmen. Closeups: tight crop on object pedestal showing the helmet promptBlock. Dramatic imagined moments use three-quarter viewpoint of the viewer_viking charging with horns exaggerated for visceral effect.
cameraLanguage.visualHierarchyRules: Objects that carry factual weight (Gjermundbu, Veksø) must be centered and occupy roughly the central third of the frame in closeups. Theatrical props or costume images are slightly offset to imply 'constructed' status.
cameraLanguage.whenEstablishingVsCloseupVsDiagram: Use establishing battlefield and theater stage scenes for the hook and spectacle; switch to museum-gallery closeups for the archaeological evidence beat; use two-panel diagrams for direct comparisons and the timeline for chronology beats.

textPolicy.exceptionsPolicy: A short (<=5 word) exact phrase may be requested directly of the image model only when it is naturally part of the drawn artwork itself (e.g. a sign, a clock face) AND the configured renderer has demonstrated adequate text fidelity for this recipe — otherwise all text is composited as a deterministic overlay after the base image.

neverDrift: the recipe's own universal style (flat 2D, uniform outline, flat fills, no shading/gradients/texture)
Do not add horns, sockets, or rivet-hole details to the Gjermundbu helmet canonicalAppearance or promptBlock.
Do not change the viewer avatars' tunic/outfit colors or hair descriptions across scenes.
Do not depict Bronze Age Veksø helmets as thick or battle-ready; they must look thin and decorative.
allowedToVary: Facial expression (open mouth for shouting, neutral for narration) for archetypes as needed.
Scale and crop of objects for closeups vs. distance shots.
episodeWideConsistencyRules: All object promptBlocks are self-contained and used verbatim for object closeups.
Setting blocks contain no humans; people are added by role archetypes per scene.

factualVisualConstraints: Show the Gjermundbu helmet as a rounded iron dome with spectacle guard and no horn attachments.
Show the Veksø helmets as thin bronze ceremonial helmets with prominent curved horns.
Do not present any authenticated Viking-age helmet with attached horns in museum closeups.
negativeRules: painterly, sketchy, or textured drift away from flat solid fills
stickman construction mutating into a more detailed/realistic character mid-episode
shading, gradients, or texture appearing despite the flat-fill policy
Never imply the Gjermundbu helmet had horn sockets or was decorative.
Never present Bronze Age horned helmets as evidence of Viking battle gear without labeling them as Bronze Age ritual objects.
Never depict a Viking-age warrior on the battlefield actually wearing the Veksø-style bronze horned helmets.
